`(2, 3)` → `(3, -2)`, first quadrant to fourth. Test with `(1, 0)`: it should land on `(0, -1)` ✓.

Rotating `(0, 4)` clockwise gives `(4, 0)`: the point travels from the positive y-axis to the positive x-axis ✓.

items.label: Rotating `(x, y)` 180° about the origin?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `(-x, -y)` — identical to reflecting through the origin, and the direction of rotation no longer matters.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Half a turn sends every point to the diametrically opposite side.

Because it equals reflection through the origin, a 180° rotation is the only rotation that is also a reflection — which is why questions can describe the same transformation in two ways.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
`(2, 3)` → `(-2, -3)`, first quadrant to third. A 270° anticlockwise turn equals 90° clockwise, so it would give `(3, -2)`.

A shape with 180° rotational symmetry, such as a parallelogram, maps onto itself — its centre is the point you rotate about.

items.label: Complementary and supplementary angles?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: **Complementary** add to 90°, **supplementary** add to 180°. C before S, 90 before 180.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Supplementary pairs appear constantly because angles on a straight line total 180°. In any right triangle the two non-right angles are complementary.

Two more facts close most diagram questions: angles on a straight line sum to 180°, and angles around a point sum to 360°. Vertical (opposite) angles are always equal.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
The complement of 35° is 55°; its supplement is 145°.

If two angles on a line are `3x` and `2x`, then `5x = 180`, so they are 108° and 72°. In a right triangle with one angle 35°, the third is 55°.

items.label: Two parallel lines cut by a transversal — which angles are equal?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Only **two** values appear, and every angle is one or the other. Corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are **equal**; co-interior (same-side) angles are **supplementary**. Vertical (opposite) angles are always equal, parallel or not.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Rather than memorising names, look at the picture: all the "acute-looking" angles are equal to each other, all the "obtuse-looking" ones are equal to each other, and one of each pair adds to 180°.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If one angle is 70°, then every angle in the figure is 70° or 110°. Angles around a point total 360°, and angles on a line total 180° — those two facts close most diagram questions.

items.label: Sum of the interior angles of an `n`-sided polygon?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `(n - 2) x 180°`. For a **regular** polygon, divide that by `n` for one angle.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Diagonals from a single vertex cut the polygon into `n - 2` triangles, each worth 180°.

The formula also runs backwards: given the angle total, `n = total/180 + 2`. And for a *regular* polygon each interior angle is `180 - 360/n`, which is often the faster route.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Hexagon: `(6-2) x 180 = 720°`, so a regular hexagon has angles of `720/6 = 120°`. A pentagon totals 540°, giving 108° each.

A polygon whose interior angles sum to 1,080° has `1080/180 + 2 = 8` sides. A regular decagon has angles of `180 - 36 = 144°`.

items.label: Sum of the exterior angles of any polygon?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Always **360°**, whatever the number of sides. For a regular polygon each exterior angle is `360/n`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Walking once round the polygon turns you through one full revolution, and at each corner you turn by the exterior angle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Regular hexagon: each exterior angle is `360/6 = 60°`, so each interior angle is `180 - 60 = 120°` ✓. If a regular polygon has exterior angles of 24°, it has `360/24 = 15` sides.

A regular polygon with interior angles of 150° has exterior angles of 30°, so it has 12 sides.

items.label: What makes a polygon regular?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: All sides equal **and** all angles equal. Both conditions are required.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Regularity is what lets you divide the angle total by `n`, and it is the condition behind the maximum-area results later.

For a regular polygon everything follows from `n`: each interior angle is `180 - 360/n`, each exterior angle is `360/n`, and the number of diagonals is `n(n-3)/2`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
A regular octagon has angles of 135°. A rhombus has equal sides but unequal angles; a rectangle has equal angles but unequal sides — neither is regular. Only the square is both.

A hexagon has `6(3)/2 = 9` diagonals; a pentagon has 5.

items.label: The quadrilateral family — how do they nest?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
- **Parallelogram**: two pairs of parallel sides; opposite sides and angles equal; diagonals bisect each other.
- **Rhombus**: parallelogram with four equal sides.
- **Rectangle**: parallelogram with four right angles.
- **Square**: both a rhombus and a rectangle.
- **Trapezoid**: exactly one pair of parallel sides, so not a parallelogram.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The hierarchy answers "must be true" questions directly: every square is a rectangle, but most rectangles are not squares.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: "A quadrilateral with four equal sides" could be a square or a non-square rhombus — ambiguous enough to make a comparison question answer D.

items.label: What does a trapezoid actually guarantee?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Only that the two angles on the same leg add to **180°**. All four sides and all four angles can otherwise be different.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Those co-interior angles are supplementary because the other two sides are parallel. Symmetry is not implied — only an *isosceles* trapezoid has equal legs and equal base angles, and the question must say so.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A base angle of 70° forces 110° directly above it on the same leg. The other leg could carry 50° and 130°, a completely different pair.

items.label: Inscribed versus circumscribed?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: **Inscribed** is drawn inside, **circumscribed** is drawn around — and in both cases every vertex of the inner shape must touch the outer shape.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The touching condition is what turns the words into measurements: a square inscribed in a circle has its **diagonal** equal to the diameter; a circle inscribed in a square has its **diameter** equal to the side.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Square inscribed in a circle of radius 5: diagonal 10, so side `10/sqrt(2) = 5sqrt(2)` and area 50. Circle inscribed in a square of side 10: radius 5, area `25pi`.

items.label: In a triangle, how do angles and opposite sides relate?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Largest angle faces the longest side, smallest angle faces the shortest side — and the ordering works both ways.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Knowing the order of the angles gives you the order of the sides for free, which is often all a comparison question needs.

Two immediate corollaries: equal angles face equal sides (so an isosceles triangle's base angles are equal), and in a right triangle the hypotenuse is always the longest side because 90° is the largest angle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
In a 30-60-90 triangle the shortest side faces the 30° and the hypotenuse faces the 90°. If `angle A > angle B`, then side `a` (opposite A) is longer than side `b`.

A triangle with angles 50°, 60°, 70° has its sides in that same order of size, so the side opposite the 50° is the shortest.

items.label: Given two sides of a triangle, what can the third be?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Strictly between their **difference** and their **sum**: `|a - b| < c < a + b`. Any two sides must together exceed the third.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Applied to all three pairs, the triangle inequality pins the missing side into a range — and questions usually ask for the number of integer possibilities.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Sides 7 and 10: `3 < x < 17`, so an integer third side has **13** possibilities (4 through 16).

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The inequality is strict. Sides 3, 7 and 10 make a flat line, not a triangle.

items.label: What proves two triangles congruent?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: **SSS**, **SAS** (angle *between* the sides), **ASA**, or **AAS**. Notably **SSA does not work** — two different triangles usually fit.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Congruent means identical in size and shape, so three well-chosen pieces pin it down. The exception matters: with two sides and a non-included angle, the third side can swing to two positions.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two triangles with sides 5 and 7 and the 40° angle between them are congruent by SAS. With the 40° opposite the 5 instead, nothing is guaranteed.

items.label: What do similar triangles give you?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Equal angles and all corresponding lengths in one fixed ratio. **Two** equal angles are enough to prove similarity. Lengths scale by `k`; **areas scale by `k^2`**.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Similar means same shape, different scale — every length (sides, heights, perimeters) uses the same factor, but area uses its square. That squared factor is the part questions target.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two triangles with angles 40-60-80; the first has its 40°-side of length 6, the second 9, a ratio of 3:2. If the first has area 20, the second has area `20 x (3/2)^2 = 45`, not 30.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Match sides by the angles they face, not by the order they are written.

items.label: Pythagorean theorem?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `a^2 + b^2 = c^2`, with `c` the hypotenuse — right triangles only.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: It is also the converse: if the three sides satisfy it, the triangle *is* right-angled. And it is the engine behind the distance formula and the diagonal of a box.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Legs 6 and 8: `36 + 64 = 100`, so `c = 10`. Backwards, hypotenuse 13 with one leg 5: `b^2 = 169 - 25 = 144`, so `b = 12`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The hypotenuse is always the longest side and always faces the right angle. Plugging it in as a leg is the standard error.

items.label: The 30-60-90 triangle — side ratios?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `1 : sqrt(3) : 2`. The short side (`x`) faces 30°, the hypotenuse (`2x`) faces 90°, the middle side (`x sqrt(3)`) faces 60°.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: It is half an equilateral triangle cut down the middle, which is also where the height of an equilateral triangle comes from.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Hypotenuse 10 → short side 5, long leg `5sqrt(3) ≈ 8.66`. So an equilateral triangle of side 10 has height `5sqrt(3)`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Match sides to angles, not to their position in the picture. Given the **long leg** as 6, the short side is `6/sqrt(3) = 2sqrt(3)`, not 3.

items.label: The 45-45-90 triangle — side ratios?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `1 : 1 : sqrt(2)`. Two equal legs, hypotenuse `sqrt(2)` times as long.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
It is a square cut along its diagonal, which is why a square of side `s` has diagonal `s sqrt(2)`.

It appears whenever a square's diagonal shows up, and in isosceles right triangles hidden inside larger figures.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Legs 5 → hypotenuse `5sqrt(2) ≈ 7.07`. Backwards: hypotenuse 10 → legs `10/sqrt(2) = 5sqrt(2)`. So a square with diagonal 10 has area 50.

A square of side 8 has diagonal `8sqrt(2) ≈ 11.3`. A 45-45-90 triangle with hypotenuse `6sqrt(2)` has legs of 6 and area 18.

items.label: A triangle with awkward angles like 30-105-45 — what do you do?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Drop a perpendicular to split it into two special right triangles. 105° splits into 45 + 60; 75° splits into 45 + 30.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Once the figure is two known triangles you can use their ratios on both halves and add the areas. Look for angles that decompose into 30/45/60.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For 30-105-45 with one side given, the height from the 105° vertex creates a 30-60-90 and a 45-45-90 sharing that height. Find the height, use each ratio for its base piece, then add the two areas.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The perpendicular must land inside the triangle for the areas to add. In an obtuse triangle it may fall outside, and you subtract instead.

items.label: Pythagorean triples worth recognising?

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Recognition saves a square root, and recognising a near-miss saves you from assuming a right angle that is not there.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Legs 8 and 15 → hypotenuse 17 instantly. Legs 9 and 12 → 15, since that is `3 x (3-4-5)`. But sides 5, 12 and 14 are **not** right-angled, however familiar the 5 and 12 look.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The largest number must be the hypotenuse.

items.label: Area of a triangle?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `area = (1/2) x base x height`, where the height is **perpendicular** to the chosen base.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Any side can be the base, as long as you use the height perpendicular to *that* side. In a right triangle the two legs are base and height already.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Base 10, height 6 → area 30. A right triangle with legs 6 and 8 has area 24 (the hypotenuse never enters). Two triangles with the same base and the same height have equal areas, however different they look.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: In an obtuse triangle the height can fall outside the triangle — it is still the perpendicular distance, not a side.

items.label: Area and perimeter of a rectangle and a square?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Rectangle: `area = lw`, `perimeter = 2(l + w)`. Square of side `s`: `area = s^2`, `perimeter = 4s`, `diagonal = s sqrt(2)`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The pairing that questions exploit: a fixed perimeter leaves the area free to vary wildly, and a fixed area leaves the perimeter free — the square is the extreme in both cases.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Perimeter 40: a 10x10 square has area 100, a 15x5 rectangle 75, a 19x1 rectangle just 19. Conversely, area 36 can be a 6x6 square (perimeter 24) or a 36x1 rectangle (perimeter 74).

items.label: Area of an equilateral triangle of side `s`?

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
It follows from the 30-60-90 ratios: the height is `s sqrt(3)/2`, and area is half base times height.

Because it depends on `s^2`, the ratio of the areas of two equilateral triangles is the square of the ratio of their sides. And six of them make a regular hexagon, which is how hexagon areas are computed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Side 6 → `(sqrt(3) x 36)/4 = 9sqrt(3) ≈ 15.6`. Doubling the side to 12 **quadruples** the area, since it depends on `s^2`.

Given an area of `25sqrt(3)`, solve `(sqrt(3)s^2)/4 = 25sqrt(3)` → `s^2 = 100` → `s = 10`. A regular hexagon of side 10 then has area `6 x 25sqrt(3) = 150sqrt(3)`.

items.label: Area of a parallelogram?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `base x height`, where the height is the **perpendicular** distance between the parallel sides — not the slanted side.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: A parallelogram is a rectangle pushed over, and pushing it over changes neither base nor height.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Base 10 with a slant side of 6 leaning at 30°: height `= 6 sin(30°) = 3`, so the area is **30**, not 60.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Using the slanted side as the height always overestimates — it is the most common area error.

items.label: Area of a trapezoid?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `((base1 + base2)/2) x height` — the average of the parallel sides times the distance between them.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
You are finding the width of the "average" rectangle. If the two bases were equal it would be a parallelogram, and the formula collapses to base times height.

It also runs backwards to find a missing base or height, which is the usual exam form: substitute what you know and solve.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Parallel sides 8 and 12, height 5 → `10 x 5 = 50`.

A trapezoid of area 60 with bases 7 and 13 has height `60 = 10h`, so `h = 6`.

items.label: Circumference and area of a circle?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `circumference = 2 pi r = pi d`, `area = pi r^2`. Radius is half the diameter.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Nearly every circle question is "find `r` first". Whatever you are given — area, circumference, a chord, an inscribed square — convert it to the radius and the rest follows.

Scaling: doubling the radius doubles the circumference but **quadruples** the area.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Radius 6: circumference `12pi ≈ 37.7`, area `36pi ≈ 113`. Given an area of `49pi`, the radius is 7 and the circumference is `14pi`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Read whether you are given radius or diameter. Using `d` where the formula wants `r` doubles or quadruples the answer.

items.label: Arc length and sector area for a central angle of `n` degrees?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Take that fraction of the whole circle:
`arc = (n/360) x 2 pi r` and `sector area = (n/360) x pi r^2`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: A sector is a slice of pizza: the central angle tells you what fraction of the full 360° you have, and both the boundary and the area scale by that same fraction.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Radius 6, central angle 60°: that is `1/6` of the circle, so the arc is `(1/6)(12pi) = 2pi` and the sector area is `(1/6)(36pi) = 6pi`. Backwards: an arc of `3pi` on a radius-6 circle is `3pi/12pi = 1/4` of the circle, so the angle is 90°.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Arc length is a distance and sector area is an area — do not use one where the other is asked.

items.label: Inscribed angles, and the angle in a semicircle?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: An inscribed angle is **half** the central angle standing on the same arc. So an angle inscribed in a semicircle (standing on a diameter) is always **90°**.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The semicircle case is the one the GRE uses most: any triangle with the diameter as one side and its third vertex on the circle is right-angled at that vertex.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A central angle of 80° gives an inscribed angle of 40° on the same arc. And if `AB` is a diameter and `C` is anywhere else on the circle, `angle ACB = 90°`, so `AC^2 + BC^2 = AB^2`.

items.label: Area of a regular polygon?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `area = (n x s x a)/2`, where `a` is the **apothem** — the perpendicular distance from the centre to the middle of a side. Since `n x s` is the perimeter, this is "half perimeter times apothem".

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The polygon splits into `n` identical triangles, each with base `s` and height `a`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Regular hexagon of side 6: apothem `3sqrt(3) ≈ 5.196`, so area `= (6 x 6 x 5.196)/2 ≈ 93.5`. Cross-check with six equilateral triangles: `6 x 9sqrt(3) = 54sqrt(3) ≈ 93.5` ✓.

items.label: A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle — how do side and radius compare?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `s = r`, exactly. Fewer sides → `s > r` (a square gives `s = r sqrt(2)`); more sides → `s < r`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
The hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles meeting at the centre, each with every side equal to the radius.

It makes several figures computable at a glance: the hexagon's perimeter is `6r`, its area is six equilateral triangles of side `r`, and its longest diagonal is the circle's diameter `2r`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Hexagon in a circle of radius 6: sides 6, perimeter 36, area `54sqrt(3) ≈ 93.5`. The circle's area is `36pi ≈ 113`, so the hexagon fills about 83% of it.

items.label: Same perimeter, different shapes — which has the most area?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: The most **regular** one, and the further from regular, the less area. Across different side counts, more sides is better, with the circle the overall winner.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Stretching a shape while keeping its perimeter loses area fast, which is what makes these comparison questions answerable without computing anything.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Perimeter 40: a 10x10 square gives 100, a 15x5 rectangle 75, a 19x1 rectangle 19. A circle of circumference 40 has area ≈127, beating every polygon.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: This is about a **fixed perimeter**. With a fixed area the comparison reverses.

items.label: Volume and surface area of a rectangular solid and a cube?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Box: `volume = lwh`, `surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh)`. Cube of side `s`: `volume = s^3`, `surface area = 6s^2`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
A box has three pairs of identical faces, which is where the 2 and the three products come from. For a cube all six faces match.

Scaling: double every edge and the volume goes up **8 times**, the surface area **4 times**.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A 3x4x5 box: volume 60, surface area `2(12 + 15 + 20) = 94`. A cube of side 4: volume 64, surface area 96.

items.label: Volume and surface area of a cylinder?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `volume = pi r^2 h`. `surface area = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h` — two circular ends plus the curved side.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The curved side unrolls into a rectangle of height `h` and width equal to the circumference `2 pi r`, which is where the second term comes from.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Radius 3, height 10: volume `= 90pi ≈ 283`; surface area `= 18pi + 60pi = 78pi ≈ 245`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Radius appears squared in the volume, so changing it has an outsized effect: doubling `r` quadruples the volume, while doubling `h` only doubles it.

items.label: Same volume, different shapes — which has the least surface area?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: The most **regular** one. Elongate a solid and the surface area climbs while the volume stays put. The sphere wins overall; among boxes, the cube.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The three-dimensional partner of the perimeter rule, and it is tested the same way — as a comparison you answer by reasoning, not calculating.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Volume 64: a 4x4x4 cube has surface area 96; a 16x2x2 box has the same volume but surface area `2(32 + 32 + 4) = 136`. A sphere of volume 64 has about 77.

items.label: What is the longest straight line that fits inside a box?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: The **space diagonal** — corner to diametrically opposite corner, crossing length, width and height at once. Not a face diagonal.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: This is the "longest rod that fits" question. The two furthest-apart points of a box are opposite corners, so both the width and the depth get "diagonalled".

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a room, the longest line runs from a bottom corner to the opposite top corner. In a 3x4x12 box the best face diagonal is only 5, while the true longest is 13.

items.label: Formula for the diagonal of a rectangular solid?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `d = sqrt(l^2 + w^2 + h^2)`. For a cube of side `s` it collapses to `s sqrt(3)`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Pythagoras applied twice: once across the base to get the floor diagonal, then again vertically using that diagonal and the height.

It is also the 3-D distance formula: the diagonal is the distance between opposite corners, exactly as `sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)` measures distance in space.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
3x4x12 box: `sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13`. Cube of side 5: `5sqrt(3) ≈ 8.66`.

A 6x6x7 box: `sqrt(36 + 36 + 49) = sqrt(121) = 11`. And "will a 12-inch rod fit in a 4x6x9 box?" → `sqrt(16+36+81) = sqrt(133) ≈ 11.5`, so no.

items.label: How many small boxes fit inside a big one?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Divide **per dimension** and round each down, then multiply. Dividing the volumes only works when every dimension divides exactly.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Volume division silently assumes the leftover slivers can be reassembled, which they cannot.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 2x2x2 cubes into a 10x10x10 box: everything divides, so `1000/8 = 125`, matching `5 x 5 x 5`. But 3x3x3 cubes: volume division suggests 37, while per dimension you fit `10/3 → 3`, giving `3 x 3 x 3 = 27`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: You may be allowed to rotate the small box. When the dimensions differ, test the orientations — one often fits noticeably more.

items.label: Mixing two solutions — what is the concentration of the result?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: A weighted average: `(ax + by)/(x + y)`, where mixture A is `a%` strong with volume `x` and B is `b%` with volume `y`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The numerator is the total amount of the important substance, the denominator the total volume. The result is pulled toward whichever mixture contributes more volume.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 30 litres of 20% acid with 10 litres of 60%: `(6 + 6)/40 = 30%`. Much closer to 20% than 60%, because there is three times as much of the weak one.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The answer must lie strictly **between** the two concentrations. Outside that range means an arithmetic slip.

items.label: What ratio of two mixtures gives a target concentration?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Alligation: take each mixture's distance from the target and **swap them**. `A : B = |z - b| : |z - a|`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The mixture further from the target contributes less, so its distance becomes the *other* one's share. No algebra needed.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Mix 20% and 60% acid to get 30%. Distances 10 and 30, swapped gives `A : B = 30 : 10 = 3 : 1`. Check: `(0.2 x 3 + 0.6 x 1)/4 = 30%` ✓.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Sanity-check which way round it goes: the mixture **nearer** the target must get the larger share.

items.label: Quartiles — what exactly is Q1, and what sits "inside" a quarter?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Quartiles cut an ordered list into four parts: Q1 has a quarter below it, Q2 is the median, Q3 has three quarters below. The quartile **values are boundaries, not members** — a value sitting exactly on Q1 belongs to neither neighbouring quarter.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The same holds for deciles and percentiles: they are dividing lines. The interquartile range `Q3 - Q1` is what the GRE usually wants, and it is robust to the small definitional differences between textbooks.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8: Q2 = 4.5, Q1 = 2.5, Q3 = 6.5, so the interquartile range is 4. "The third quarter" means the values strictly between Q2 and Q3 — 5 and 6.

items.label: Variance — how is it built?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `variance = sum of (term - mean)^2 / N`. Distance from the mean, squared, averaged.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Squaring stops positives and negatives cancelling, and it makes outliers count heavily — a term twice as far from the mean contributes four times as much.

Variance is in *squared* units, which is why standard deviation — its square root — is the figure actually quoted. A variance of 0 means every value is identical.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
For 2, 4, 6: mean 4; differences -2, 0, 2; squares 4, 0, 4; total 8; `8/3 ≈ 2.67`.

For 10, 10, 10 the variance is 0. For 8, 10, 12 the mean is 10, the squared differences are 4, 0, 4, and the variance is 8/3 — the same as for 2, 4, 6, since only the spread matters, not the location.

items.label: Standard deviation — the procedure?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: The square root of the variance: (1) find the mean, (2) subtract it from each term, (3) square the differences, (4) add them, (5) divide by `N`, (6) square root.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Taking the root brings the measure back into the units of the data, which is why SD rather than variance is what questions quote.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 2, 4, 6 → variance 2.67 → SD ≈ **1.63**. The list 1, 4, 7 has the same mean but more spread, giving `sqrt(6) ≈ 2.45`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Most GRE questions only ask you to **compare** SDs, which you can often do by eye: the list whose values sit further from the mean wins, no arithmetic needed.

items.label: Population versus sample standard deviation?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Population divides by `N`; sample divides by `N - 1`. The sample version is slightly larger.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Dividing by a smaller number compensates for a sample tending to understate the spread of the population it came from. The GRE means population SD unless it says "sample".

The intuition for `N - 1`: a sample's own mean sits closer to its points than the true population mean does, so the squared differences come out slightly too small, and the smaller divisor corrects for it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
For 2, 4, 6: population SD `= sqrt(8/3) ≈ 1.63`; sample SD `= sqrt(8/2) = 2`.

The gap shrinks as the sample grows: with `N = 100` the two divisors differ by 1%, which is why the distinction rarely changes a comparison answer.

items.label: Add 10 to every value, or multiply every value by 3 — what happens to the SD?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Adding or subtracting a constant: **no change**. Multiplying or dividing: the SD is multiplied or divided by the same factor.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Adding shifts the whole list without changing the gaps; multiplying stretches the gaps. The mean, by contrast, changes under both.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 2, 4, 6 has SD ≈ 1.63. Adding 100 gives 102, 104, 106 — SD still 1.63, mean now 104. Multiplying by 3 gives 6, 12, 18 — SD ≈ 4.90.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Variance scales by the **square** of the factor: multiplying the list by 3 multiplies the variance by 9.

items.label: Standardizing a list (z-scores)?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `z = (value - mean)/SD`. Subtract the mean from every value, then divide by the SD. The new list always has mean 0 and SD 1.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: A z-score says how many standard deviations a value sits from the mean, which is what lets you compare positions across different scales.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The list 2, 8 has mean 5 and population SD 3, so it standardizes to -1 and 1. A score of 8 is "one standard deviation above the mean".

items.label: The normal distribution — what percentages should you be able to draw?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: **2 / 14 / 34 / 34 / 14 / 2**. So about 68% lies within 1 SD of the mean, about 96% within 2 SDs, and about 4% beyond 2 SDs.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The curve is symmetric, so each half holds 50%: `34 + 14 + 2 = 50` is the check you use when reconstructing the sketch from memory.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Scores are normal with mean 500, SD 100. Between 400 and 600: 68%. Above 700: 2%. Between 600 and 700: 14%. A score of 700 is roughly the 98th percentile, since `50 + 34 + 14 = 98`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Draw the curve and write the six numbers under it before answering. Almost every normal-distribution question is then just reading off the sketch.

items.label: Data interpretation questions — what should you do before calculating?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Read the **axes, units and footnotes** first: what exactly is being measured, in what units, and is the chart showing an amount or a percentage of something.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
The arithmetic in a DI set is easy; the traps are in the reading. Percentages of different bases cannot be added or compared directly, and "percent" versus "percentage points" are different questions.

A set of questions shares one chart, so the time spent understanding it pays back three times. Estimate first — answer choices are usually far apart.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A bar chart shows revenue in **thousands** and a pie chart shows each region's **share**. "Which region grew most?" is about the bars; "which had the largest share?" is about the pie — and a region can gain share while its revenue falls, if the total fell faster.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: A percentage increase from 5% to 10% is a rise of 5 percentage **points** but a 100% **increase**.

items.label: Set versus list — what is the difference?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: A **set** is unordered with no duplicates, written `{2, 5, 9}`, and can be infinite; its size is `|S|`. A **list** is ordered, allows duplicates, and is finite.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The distinction decides which tool applies: sets lead to combinations and inclusion–exclusion, lists lead to permutations.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: `{1, 2, 3}` and `{3, 2, 1}` are the same set, but the lists (1, 2, 3) and (3, 2, 1) differ. `{1, 1, 2}` is just `{1, 2}` with two elements, while the list (1, 1, 2) has three entries.

items.label: Inclusion–exclusion for two groups?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `|A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|` — add the two, subtract the overlap you counted twice.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The rearranged form is the one exams use: knowing the total and both groups gives you the overlap.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 30 students, 18 take French, 15 Spanish, everyone takes at least one. `30 = 18 + 15 - both` → **3** take both. If 4 took neither, use `30 - 4 = 18 + 15 - both` → 7.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Check whether the total includes people in **neither** group — remove them before applying the formula.

items.label: Inclusion–exclusion for three groups?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
`|A or B or C| = |A| + |B| + |C| - |A and B| - |B and C| - |A and C| + |A and B and C|`

If instead you are told how many are in **exactly** two groups:
`total = |A| + |B| + |C| - (exactly two) - 2 x (all three)`

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The pairwise subtractions remove the triple overlap once too often, so the standard version adds it back. Which formula you need depends entirely on the wording, so settle that first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 40 students: 20 football, 18 basketball, 16 tennis, 8 football+basketball, 6 basketball+tennis, 5 football+tennis, 3 all three. `20+18+16-8-6-5+3 = 38` play at least one, so 2 play none.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: "8 play football and basketball" normally means *at least* those two, including anyone who also plays tennis. "Only football and basketball" is the other formula.

items.label: Several independent choices in a row — how many outcomes?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Multiply the options at each stage: `a x b x c ...`

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
The multiplication principle is the backbone of every counting question; extend it to as many stages as you like.

It also covers repeats: choosing from `n` options `r` times **with** repetition gives `n^r`, because every stage still has all `n` options available.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
4 starters and 3 mains → 12 meals; add 2 desserts → 24. A 4-digit PIN from 10 digits with repeats allowed → `10^4 = 10,000`.

A 3-letter code from 26 letters with repeats allowed: `26^3 = 17,576`. Without repeats: `26 x 25 x 24 = 15,600`.

items.label: When do you add possibilities, and when do you multiply?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: **AND → multiply** (both stages happen). **OR → add** (one or the other, not both).

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Label each branch of the problem before computing; most complex counting questions are just a tree of these two operations.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A to B by 3 roads then B to C by 4 roads: both legs needed → `3 x 4 = 12` routes. But if you may go to C by one of 3 roads **or** one of 4 others → `3 + 4 = 7`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: If "or" allows both to happen, adding double-counts — go back to inclusion–exclusion.

items.label: Optional extras, and "at least one" — how do you count them?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Each optional item is a two-way choice (in or out), so `n` options give `2^n` combinations. For "at least one", count everything and **subtract the case where nothing was chosen**.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Count-all-then-subtract-the-bad-case is the standard move for "at least" questions, and it is almost always faster than counting the good cases.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 4 ice-cream flavours with 4 optional toppings: `4 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 64`. If at least one topping is compulsory, remove the 4 no-topping cases: **60**.

items.label: Choosing `r` from `n` where order does **not** matter?

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The `r!` divides out the orderings of the same chosen group — which is exactly what "order does not matter" means. Note the symmetry `nCr = nC(n-r)`: choosing 3 to include is choosing 7 to exclude.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 3-person committees from 10 people: `10C3 = (10 x 9 x 8)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 120`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The giveaway words are committee, group, handshake, selection — anything where swapping two members changes nothing.

items.label: Choosing `r` from `n` where order **does** matter?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `nPr = n!/(n - r)!` — which is `nCr` times `r!`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Each chosen group can be arranged in `r!` ways, so permutations always outnumber combinations by that factor.

The relationship is worth holding onto: `nPr = nCr x r!`. Whenever you can count the groups, multiply by `r!` to get the ordered count.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Gold, silver, bronze among 10 runners: `10P3 = 10 x 9 x 8 = 720`, six times the 120 committees, because each trio can stand on the podium in `3! = 6` orders.

Arranging 2 of 5 books on a shelf: `5P2 = 20`. Choosing 2 of 5 to take on holiday: `5C2 = 10` — exactly half, since each pair has `2! = 2` orders.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Ranking, order, podium, "president and treasurer", password → permutation.

items.label: Counting arrangements without any formula?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: The **slot method**: draw a blank for each position, write how many options it has, multiply. Each item used reduces the next slot by one.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
It is the formula in disguise, but far harder to misapply — and it extends naturally to restricted positions.

The slot method is also the only practical approach once restrictions appear, because you can fill the constrained slots first and let the rest follow.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Arranging ABCDE: `5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120`, matching `5P5`. Taking only the first three letters: `5 x 4 x 3 = 60 = 5P3`.

How many 3-digit numbers have no repeated digits? The first slot cannot be 0, so `9 x 9 x 8 = 648`.

items.label: Arrangements with a restriction on some positions?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Fill the **restricted slots first**, then the rest by the slot method. Separate scenarios are **added**; simultaneous stages are **multiplied**.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Two standard tricks: to keep items **together**, glue them into one block and arrange the blocks (then multiply by the arrangements inside the block); to keep items **apart**, count everything and subtract the arrangements where they are together.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 4-digit numbers from 1–7, no repeats, must be even. The last slot must be 2, 4 or 6 → 3 options; the other three slots take the remaining digits → `6 x 5 x 4 = 120`. Total `3 x 120 = 360`.

items.label: Arranging `n` items when some are identical?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `n!/(a! b! ...)`, dividing by the factorial of each repeat count.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Swapping two identical items produces no new arrangement, so the plain `n!` overcounts by exactly those internal orderings.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: BANANA: `n = 6` with three As and two Ns → `6!/(3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60`. A word with no repeats, like ABCDEF, keeps the full `6! = 720`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Divide by each repeat's factorial **separately**: three As and two Ns means `3! x 2! = 12`, not `5!`.

items.label: Repeats **and** restrictions together?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: Split the problem into the sections the restriction creates, count each with the repeats formula, then multiply the sections (or add, if they are alternatives).

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Handle one constraint at a time and the hardest-looking counting questions become two small ones.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Arrangements of TEXTBOOK with all vowels first and all consonants last. Vowels E, O, O → `3!/2! = 3`. Consonants T, X, T, B, K → `5!/2! = 60`. Both blocks are required, so `3 x 60 = 180`.

items.label: An unfamiliar counting question — what do you ask yourself first?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Three questions: **how many items**, **how many are being chosen or arranged**, and **does order matter**? Then a fourth: are repeats allowed?

Order matters → permutation. Order does not → combination. Repeats allowed → plain multiplication (`n^r`). Identical items → divide by the repeat factorials.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Nearly every counting question is one of the standard types in disguise. Answering those three questions names the type, and then the formula is mechanical.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: "5 books on a shelf, 2 identical" → arranging 5, order matters, one repeat of 2 → `5!/2! = 60`. "3-topping pizzas from 8 toppings" → choosing 3 of 8, order irrelevant → `8C3 = 56`.

items.label: Seating `n` people around a **circular** table?

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: A circle has no fixed starting point, so rotating everyone one seat gives the same arrangement — each distinct seating was counted `n` times, and `n!/n = (n-1)!`. In practice: fix one person, then arrange the rest around them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 5 people in a row: `5! = 120`. The same 5 around a table: `4! = 24`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Numbered seats make it a row again, and a flippable arrangement (a bracelet) halves the count. Read the setup carefully.

items.label: For a fixed `n`, which `r` makes `nCr` largest?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `r = n/2`. If `n` is odd, the two values either side of the middle tie.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Choosing about half the items gives the most possible groups; the counts fall away symmetrically toward `r = 0` and `r = n`, which each have exactly one.

items.label: Basic probability of an event?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes`, always between 0 and 1. All the outcomes you count must be **equally likely**.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Most probability questions are really counting questions wearing a hat — build the numerator and denominator with the counting tools you already have.

`P(not E) = 1 - P(E)` is the other half of the toolkit.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: One card from a deck: `P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13`. Two dice: `P(sum of 7) = 6/36 = 1/6`, since 6 of the 36 equally likely pairs total 7. Choosing 2 people from 10 of whom 4 are women, `P(both women) = 4C2 / 10C2 = 6/45 = 2/15`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Equally likely matters. The sums of two dice are **not** equally likely — 7 comes up six times as often as 2.

items.label: Probability that A **and** B both happen?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: For **independent** events, `P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)`. If they are not independent, use `P(A) x P(B given A)`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Independence means one event does not change the odds of the other. "Without replacement" is the standard flag that it fails.

For three or more independent events, keep multiplying. For dependent ones, each factor is conditioned on everything before it.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
Two coin flips both heads: `1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4`. Two aces drawn without replacement: `4/52 x 3/51 = 1/221`, **not** `(4/52)^2`.

Three heads in a row: `(1/2)^3 = 1/8`. Three aces without replacement: `4/52 x 3/51 x 2/50 = 1/5,525`.

items.label: Probability that A **or** B happens?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)` — inclusion–exclusion again.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Adding the two probabilities double-counts the outcomes where both occur, so the overlap comes off once.

When the events are mutually exclusive the overlap is 0, so the formula collapses to plain addition — which is why "or" questions about outcomes that cannot co-occur feel so much easier.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text:
One die: `P(even) = 3/6`, `P(>3) = 3/6`, overlap {4, 6} `= 2/6`. So `P(even or >3) = 3/6 + 3/6 - 2/6 = 2/3`, matching the list 2, 4, 5, 6.

Drawing a king **or** a queen: mutually exclusive, so `4/52 + 4/52 = 2/13`. Drawing a king **or** a heart: they overlap in the king of hearts, so `4/52 + 13/52 - 1/52 = 4/13`.

items.label: Independent versus mutually exclusive — what is the difference?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: **Independent**: neither affects the other, so `P(A and B) = P(A)P(B)`. **Mutually exclusive**: they cannot both happen, so `P(A and B) = 0` and `P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: They sound similar and mean opposite things. A consequence worth remembering: for mutually exclusive events `P(A) + P(B) <= 1`, since probabilities summing past 1 would force an overlap.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two coin flips are independent (both can be heads). One card being both a king and a queen is mutually exclusive. Two events with non-zero probability can never be both — if they cannot co-occur, knowing one happened tells you a great deal about the other.

items.label: Conditional probability `P(A | B)`?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: `P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)` — the probability of A **given that** B happened.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Conditioning on B shrinks the world to the outcomes where B occurred, so you rescale by dividing by `P(B)`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Roll a die: what is `P(2 | even)`? `P(2 and even) = 1/6`, `P(even) = 1/2`, so `(1/6)/(1/2) = 1/3` — matching the intuition that among 2, 4, 6 exactly one is a 2.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: `P(A | B)` and `P(B | A)` are different numbers: the probability of being even **given** a roll of 2 is 1, not 1/3.

items.label: Probability of "at least one" — what is the fast route?

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text: The complement: `P(at least one) = 1 - P(none)`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Counting directly means adding the cases for exactly one, exactly two, exactly three … The complement is a single multiplication.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Four coin flips, at least one head: `P(no heads) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16`, so the answer is **15/16**. Rolling two dice, at least one 6: `1 - (5/6)^2 = 11/36`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The complement of "at least one" is "none" — and the complement of "at least two" is "zero or one", so both cases must come off.
